Marathon Petroleum's stock fell 1% today and has slumped 11.5% over two weeks, driven primarily by a sharp collapse in oil prices. Brent crude (the global benchmark) dipped below $90 per barrel on November 10th—the lowest level since August—after President Trump signaled that the Iran conflict could end "fairly soon." For a refiner like Marathon, lower crude prices cut into profits on two fronts: the company earns less on the refined products it sells (gasoline, diesel), and it also loses the benefit of buying cheaper feedstock to process, since refinery margins depend heavily on the spread between crude input costs and output prices.

The broader headwind is geopolitical de-escalation in the Middle East. Oil prices had been elevated by war risk; as that risk recedes, crude falls. At the same time, the midterm elections showed strong voter support for renewable energy over fossil fuels, which adds longer-term pressure on energy demand expectations. Refineries are running at 94.5% capacity—a healthy level—but that utilization gains the company little if the price gap it operates on keeps shrinking.
